items.quote: By his side lived Govinda, his ____, walked the same paths, undertook the same efforts.
items.explain: Govinda as Siddhartha's 'shadow' sets up the friendship that the whole novel will test.

items.quote: long nails grew slowly on his parched fingers and a dry, shaggy ____ grew on his chin.
items.explain: His wild beard shows how completely he has given up caring for his body.

items.quote: And he shook his ____.
items.explain: A silent head-shake is Siddhartha's answer to Govinda's verse: doubt without words.

items.quote: How old, would you think, is our oldest Samana, our venerable teacher?
items.explain: Siddhartha's simple question about age is the start of his proof that the Samana path fails.

items.quote: Your willingness delights my heart.
items.explain: Govinda is glad his friend will come to hear the Buddha with him.

items.quote: Quickly, you’ve learned every exercise
items.explain: Govinda praises his friend's speed; Siddhartha will soon say speed proves nothing.

cards.text: News of Gotama, the Buddha, reaches the friends
Siddhartha gives his clothes to a poor Brahmin
Siddhartha casts a spell on the old Samana

items.explain: The chapter moves from giving everything up, to hearing of the Buddha, to leaving.

cards.text: Siddhartha agrees to go and hear the Buddha
Govinda asks to go and hear the Buddha
The Samanas accept the two young men

items.explain: Joining, hearing news, deciding to go: three years among the Samanas in three steps.

cards.text: Govinda guesses the oldest Samana is about sixty
The oldest Samana becomes angry
Siddhartha's soul flies as a heron

items.explain: Practice comes first, then questions, then the break with the teacher.

items.quote: The old man became **mute**, his eyes became motionless
items.explain: Siddhartha's spell silences the teacher who had just been shouting at him.

items.quote: Might we get closer to **salvation**?
items.explain: Siddhartha wants to be set free from suffering, not just to learn more exercises.

items.quote: Govinda was **startled** and became embarrassed.
items.explain: Govinda's alarm shows how unexpected Siddhartha's daring is.

items.quote: was an animal, was carrion, was stone, was wood, was water
items.link: Forms Siddhartha's soul took: a heron, a dead jackal, 'stone' (¶6). No tiger appears.
items.explain: Siddhartha's soul takes many forms in meditation.

items.quote: He fasted for fifteen days.
items.link: Siddhartha's self-denial: fasting, giving away his garments, eating once a day (¶2). He never feasted.
items.explain: Each true choice is a way Siddhartha gave up comfort.

items.quote: surrounded by disciples, without possession, without home
items.link: How the rumour pictures Gotama: disciples, no home, a yellow cloak (¶28). No crown.
items.explain: The rumoured Buddha lives simply, yet cheerfully.

items.quote: They were accepted.

verdict.claim: The Samanas accepted Siddhartha and Govinda.

items.explain: The friends' journey begins with the Samanas saying yes.

items.quote: But Siddhartha remained silent.

verdict.claim: Siddhartha argued loudly after Govinda's verse.

items.explain: His silence is thinking, not shouting; he weighs Govinda's words before he answers.

items.quote: He informed the oldest one with all the courtesy and modesty becoming to a younger one and a student.

verdict.claim: Siddhartha told the oldest Samana politely that he was leaving.

items.explain: Siddhartha leaves politely; the anger in this scene is the teacher's, not the student's.

items.quote: until nothing ____ any more
items.explain: He endures until the pain goes silent: the Samanas try to quiet the body itself.

contentFlag.context: Siddhartha endures sun, cold and thorns as a religious austerity; the chapter itself judges these practices a dead end (paras 7, 13).
contentFlag.teacherNote: Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

items.quote: It is hard, it is very hard to cast a ____ on an old Samana.
items.explain: Govinda is amazed by a power that Siddhartha has stopped caring about.

items.quote: and I have asked the holy ____, year after year
items.explain: He has questioned scripture itself for years, and his thirst remains.

items.quote: How could you have learned meditation, holding your breath
items.explain: Govinda cannot imagine Samana skills learned anywhere but with the Samanas.

items.quote: Whether he has also other and better things to give us, O friend, let us await with calm hearts.
items.explain: Siddhartha goes to the Buddha calmly, without expecting too much.

items.quote: Your willingness delights my heart.
items.explain: Govinda is glad his friend will come to hear the Buddha.

cards.text: Govinda says the circle is a spiral
Siddhartha learns to slow his heartbeat
Govinda mumbles a verse from an Upanishad

items.explain: Training, then debate, then Govinda turning to scripture for comfort.

cards.text: A rumour of Gotama reaches them
Siddhartha compares meditation to rice wine
Govinda predicts Siddhartha will be a holy man

items.explain: Govinda's hope, Siddhartha's doubt, then news of a new path.

cards.text: Govinda hears of the Buddha in a village
Siddhartha asks how old their teacher is
Govinda says Siddhartha learned more than he knew

items.explain: A question about age leads, in the end, to a new journey.

items.quote: our oldest Samana, our **venerable** teacher?
items.explain: Siddhartha honours his teacher even while doubting what he teaches.

items.quote: among so many **austere** and venerable Samanas
items.explain: Govinda points to the Samanas' strictness as proof they must be right.

items.quote: Everywhere where the **rumour** of Buddha was heard
items.explain: The Buddha first spreads through the land as talk passed on, not as fact.

items.quote: And Siddhartha said quietly, as if he was talking to himself: “What is meditation?
items.link: The practices Siddhartha calls 'fleeing from the self': meditation, fasting, holding one's breath (¶13). Begging is not on his list.
items.explain: Siddhartha lists the Samanas' practices to question them.

items.quote: He went the way of self-denial by means of pain, through voluntarily suffering and overcoming pain, hunger, thirst, tiredness.
items.link: The way of self-denial by means of pain goes through 'pain, hunger, thirst, tiredness' (¶7). Riches are not on the list.
items.explain: The Samana way of self-denial works through hardship, not wealth.

items.quote: he had performed miracles, had overcome the devil
items.link: What believers said of Gotama (¶30): remembered past lives, miracles, overcame the devil. 'Luxury' is what his enemies said.
items.explain: Believers and enemies tell different stories about Gotama.

items.quote: often the old Samanas have admired you

verdict.claim: Govinda says the old Samanas have often admired Siddhartha.

items.explain: Govinda's praise shows how well Siddhartha succeeds on a path he is about to leave.

items.quote: he had no high opinion of this Gotama

verdict.claim: The oldest Samana thought highly of Gotama.

items.explain: The old teacher distrusts the rival whose fame will take his students.

items.quote: the young men listened up, felt a longing, felt hope

verdict.claim: News of the Buddha made young men in India feel hope.

items.explain: The rumour answers a hunger many young seekers share.

items.quote: But the most important thing, the path of paths, we will not ____.
items.explain: All their feats and comfort miss the one thing that matters: the path of paths stays unfound.

items.quote: But his enemies and disbelievers said, this Gotama was a vain ____
items.explain: Only the enemies speak here; the rumour about Gotama carries blame as well as praise.

items.quote: in the yellow ____ of an ascetic
items.explain: A simple yellow cloak marks Gotama as an ascetic who owns nothing.

items.quote: You’re mocking me. Mock me if you like
items.explain: Govinda knows his friend's teasing, and stands up to it.

items.quote: Let us eat this fruit and wait for the rest
items.explain: Siddhartha values the Buddha's news mostly because it gets them moving.

items.quote: But have you not also developed a desire, an eagerness, to hear these teachings?
items.explain: Govinda sees that his doubting friend wants to hear the Buddha too.

cards.text: Govinda says they will keep learning
Siddhartha predicts no Samana will reach nirvana
Govinda fears for the holiness of prayer
Siddhartha says he has never been a drunkard

items.explain: The friends' talks grow sharper each time, until Govinda is afraid.

cards.text: Govinda recites an Upanishad verse
Siddhartha tells the oldest Samana he is leaving
Gotama's name is heard with praise and defamation
Siddhartha says he did not know Govinda's heart

items.explain: Scripture, rumour, friendship, departure: the chapter's turn in four steps.

cards.text: Siddhartha asks if they live in a circle
Every way out of the self leads back to it
Siddhartha agrees to hear the Buddha's teachings
Siddhartha's goal is to become empty

items.explain: From a goal of emptiness to the doubt that sends him on.

items.quote: there among these **wretched** people?
items.explain: Govinda looks down on tavern people; Siddhartha sees they seek the same escape.

items.quote: his will was **paralysed**
items.explain: The teacher who taught control is himself controlled.

items.quote: through imagining the mind to be **void** of all conceptions
items.explain: An empty mind is the Samana goal; the chapter shows it never lasts.

items.quote: The myth of Buddha sounded sweet.
items.link: The Buddha rumour is a 'fragrant myth' (¶30) that 'sounded sweet' with 'the scent of magic' (¶31); 'bitter' is how the world tasted to Siddhartha (¶2).
items.explain: The rumour is pictured with pleasant senses; the world itself tastes sour.

items.quote: without possession, without home, without a wife
items.link: The rumour says Gotama lives 'without possession, without home, without a wife', yet 'surrounded by disciples' (¶28).
items.explain: The Buddha is rumoured to own nothing, yet many follow him.

items.quote: But Siddhartha’s thoughts brought the Samana under their control, he had to carry out what they commanded.
items.link: The oldest Samana grows angry and swears (¶39), then bows and blesses (¶41). Walking on water is only Govinda's guess (¶42).
items.explain: The old Samana's angry and then spellbound acts frame the farewell.

items.quote: how do you think did we progress? Did we reach any goals?

verdict.claim: On a begging walk, Siddhartha claims they have already reached their goals.

items.explain: Siddhartha asks, he does not boast; his doubt about progress starts the friends' long debate.

items.quote: I am willing to listen to these teachings

verdict.claim: Siddhartha agrees to hear Gotama, though he distrusts teachings.

items.explain: Siddhartha goes to Gotama while doubting all teachers, which foreshadows the next chapter.

items.quote: And the young men returned the bows with thanks, returned the wish, went on their way with salutations.

verdict.claim: The friends left the old Samana without a word of farewell.

items.explain: The friends leave courteously, even after the spell; good manners frame the break.

items.quote: I can’t help but feel that it is not like this, my ____.
items.explain: Siddhartha opens his hardest doubt gently, as a friend, before his sharpest words to Govinda.

contentFlag.context: Later in this paragraph (¶11) Siddhartha names a red-light district of taverns; the word he uses for brothels is crude and dated (today: brothel). He uses it to show contempt for city life and to provoke Govinda.
contentFlag.teacherNote: Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

items.quote: once every desire and every urge was ____ in the heart
items.explain: Silence of desire is the Samana hope that Siddhartha will test and reject.

items.quote: He thought about the words which Govinda had said to him and thought the words through to their ____.
items.explain: Siddhartha follows Govinda's words to their end and finds that they do not hold.

items.quote: The scent of ____ flowed from these reports.
items.explain: The rumour enchants before it informs; 'magic' warns us to weigh it.

items.quote: no one will find the path of paths?
items.explain: Govinda repeats Siddhartha's phrase as a horrified question; the friends' echo shows their split.

items.quote: It is hard, it is very hard to cast a spell on an old Samana.
items.explain: Govinda admires the feat; Siddhartha dismisses it in the next breath.

items.quote: The myth of Buddha sounded sweet.
items.explain: The narrator, not a character, lets us feel the rumour's pull.

cards.text: He doubts that learning is possible at all
He asks if they live in a circle
Siddhartha asks if they have reached any goals
He says Gotama's first gift is calling them away

items.explain: Siddhartha's questions harden into conclusions, and conclusions into action.

cards.text: The Buddha rumour is compared to news in a plague
Govinda reminds Siddhartha he planned to leave
Siddhartha's spell holds the old Samana
The oldest Samana dislikes the rumour

items.explain: The rumour spreads, meets resistance, then pulls the friends away.

cards.text: His soul enters a heron
He stands in the sun until he feels no pain
The world tastes bitter to Siddhartha
He and Govinda beg in the villages

items.explain: Disgust, endurance, meditation, routine: the shape of Samana life.

contentFlag.context: Siddhartha endures sun, cold and thorns as a religious austerity; the chapter itself judges these practices a dead end (paras 7, 13).
contentFlag.teacherNote: Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

items.quote: this Gotama was a **vain** seducer
items.explain: Here 'vain' means conceited, not 'in vain': the enemies attack Gotama's character, not his success.

items.quote: with all the courtesy and modesty **becoming** to a younger one
items.explain: Siddhartha leaves politely; the teacher, not the student, loses his temper.

items.quote: when he brought news of him, the **exalted** one, the Sakyamuni
items.explain: 'Exalted' marks how followers revere Gotama before we ever meet him.

items.quote: At this, Siddhartha laughed in his very own manner, in which his voice assumed a touch of sadness and a touch of mockery
items.link: Siddhartha 'laughed', his voice with 'a touch of sadness and a touch of mockery' (¶36). No fury.
items.explain: Siddhartha's reply blends laughter, grief and irony, but no rage.

items.quote: pain, hunger, thirst, tiredness
items.link: The way of self-denial 'by means of pain': 'pain, hunger, thirst, tiredness' (¶7). Prayer is not listed.
items.explain: The Samana way of self-denial works through bodily suffering.

items.quote: what is holy, what is precious, what is venerable on earth
items.link: Govinda fears for prayer, the Brahmins' venerability and the Samanas' holiness (¶23). Gotama is not in his list.
items.explain: Govinda fears losing the old holy order, not a new teacher.

items.quote: Always, O Govinda, I had thought, Govinda would stay with the Samanas

verdict.claim: Siddhartha had expected Govinda to stay with the Samanas.

items.explain: Siddhartha, so sure about ideas, misread his closest friend.

items.quote: They rarely talked about it, because the oldest one of the Samanas did not like this myth.

verdict.claim: The friends avoided the topic partly because their teacher disliked the myth.

items.explain: Hope about the Buddha stays half-hidden under their teacher's disapproval.

items.quote: But Siddhartha remained silent.

verdict.claim: Siddhartha answered Govinda's verse with a long speech.

items.explain: His silence is thinking, not agreement.

items.quote: to find tranquility with an ____ heart
items.explain: Peace through an 'emptied' heart is the Samana goal Siddhartha later rejects.

items.quote: let us await with ____ hearts.
items.explain: Calm waiting, not eager faith: Siddhartha already holds teachers at a distance.

items.quote: without power, he had fallen victim to Siddhartha’s ____.
items.explain: Siddhartha masters the Samana arts at the moment he walks away from them.

items.quote: So now you, my faithful friend, want to take a new path
items.explain: Siddhartha is surprised that the follower is leading the way.

items.quote: your words stir up fear in my heart.
items.explain: For Govinda, doubt threatens everything holy.

items.quote: But tell me, how should this be possible?
items.explain: Govinda wants reasons; Siddhartha answers with a riddle about fruit.

cards.text: He will turn seventy and eighty
Perhaps not a single Samana will reach nirvana
Govinda and I will grow just as old
He says their feats only fool other people
Their teacher has lived sixty years without nirvana

items.explain: Siddhartha builds from one old man to a verdict on every Samana.

cards.text: His thirst has stayed as strong as ever
He might as well have asked a hornbill-bird
Siddhartha says he will soon leave the Samanas
He has asked Brahmins, Vedas and Samanas
He denies that 'learning' exists

items.explain: From a personal confession to a sweeping paradox about learning.

cards.text: Believers say Gotama reached nirvana
Many set out to seek the healer
News spreads of a man whose word can heal
Enemies call Gotama a vain seducer
A plague breaks out in a land

items.explain: The simile first builds hope, then the narrator lets doubt speak too.

items.quote: was an animal, was **carrion**, was stone
items.explain: Becoming carrion pushes self-escape to its grim limit.

items.quote: his mouth twitched with **contempt**
items.explain: His scorn for city life shows the bitterness of his ascetic years.

items.quote: this **alleged** Buddha used to be an ascetic before
items.explain: The old Samana's word 'alleged' shows his doubt about Gotama.

items.quote: The old man became mute, his eyes became motionless, his will was paralysed
items.link: He 'became mute', 'his eyes became motionless', 'his will was paralysed' (¶41). Memory is not mentioned.
items.explain: The spell stills the teacher's voice, eyes and will.

items.quote: The scent of magic flowed from these reports.
items.link: ¶31 calls the news 'The myth of Buddha', 'these reports' and 'the rumour of Buddha'; never a prophecy.
items.explain: The narrator's words for Gotama's story all mean unproven tales.

items.quote: he slipped out of his self into thousands of other forms
items.link: He 'was an animal, was carrion, was stone, was wood, was water' (¶6). Never fire.
items.explain: The forms he takes in meditation span living, dead and lifeless things.

items.quote: the son of a Brahmin from Magadha, who has seen the Buddha with his own eyes

verdict.claim: Govinda's news comes from a Brahmin's son who had seen the Buddha himself.

items.explain: Second-hand witness turns rumour into a call to go and see for themselves.

items.quote: among so many learned men, among so many Brahmins

verdict.claim: Govinda's objection rests on how many holy men are searching.

items.explain: Govinda argues from numbers and reverence; Siddhartha argues from results.

items.quote: They rarely talked about it

verdict.claim: The friends often discussed the Buddha rumour openly.

items.explain: Hope about the Buddha stays half-hidden under their teacher's disapproval.

items.quote: the earth-coloured, ____ cloak
items.explain: A plain, unsewn cloak marks his rejection of every comfort (the edition spells it 'unsown'; today: unsewn).

items.quote: to be open to ____ in unselfish thoughts
items.explain: He hopes emptiness will open him to wonders; the chapter tests that hope.

items.quote: Siddhartha practised self-denial, practised ____, according to the Samana rules.
items.explain: Self-denial and meditation are the two Samana paths that the chapter tests.

items.quote: how do you think did we progress?
items.explain: Siddhartha's first doubting question opens the friends' long debate.

items.quote: insensitivity against hunger and pain
items.explain: Govinda counts the Samanas' achievements; Siddhartha questions their worth.

items.quote: Unexpressable by words is his blissfulness of his heart.
items.explain: Govinda answers doubt by reciting an Upanishad, scripture rather than argument.

cards.text: His soul becomes a heron
He wakes to find his old self again
His soul returns, having died and decayed
His soul enters a dead jackal
He kills his senses and memory

items.explain: Each escape ends where it began, in the self.

cards.text: He learns to breathe sparingly
He stands under the burning sun
His soul enters a heron
He cowers in thorny bushes
He stands in the rainy season

items.explain: The trials move from enduring the world to leaving the body.

contentFlag.context: Siddhartha endures sun, cold and thorns as a religious austerity; the chapter itself judges these practices a dead end (paras 7, 13).
contentFlag.teacherNote: Teacher note: some schools' guidelines may treat this passage differently.

cards.text: The old man bows and blesses them
Siddhartha whispers to Govinda
The Samana swears loudly
Govinda mentions walking on water
Siddhartha tells the oldest Samana politely

items.explain: Courtesy, anger, a whisper, a spell: a farewell full of irony.

items.quote: went on their way with **salutations**
items.explain: From Latin salutare, 'to greet': the friends leave with courtesy despite everything.

items.quote: developed a desire, an **eagerness**, to hear these teachings
items.explain: Govinda names the longing Siddhartha will not admit.

items.quote: a touch of sadness and a touch of **mockery**
items.explain: Mockery mixed with sadness is the signature of Siddhartha's voice in this chapter.

items.quote: so many who are searching, so many who are eagerly trying, so many holy men
items.link: Govinda's 'so many': learned men, Brahmins, holy men (¶21). No kings.
items.explain: Govinda's crowd of witnesses are all seekers.

items.quote: Might we get closer to enlightenment? Might we get closer to salvation?
items.link: 'might we be on the right path? … closer to enlightenment? … closer to salvation?' (¶16). Gotama is not yet named.
items.explain: Siddhartha's questions name spiritual goals, not a person.

items.quote: long nails grew slowly on his parched fingers and a dry, shaggy beard grew on his chin
items.link: ¶2: 'enlarged eyes', 'long nails', 'a dry, shaggy beard'. No shaved head.
items.explain: His body shows neglect, not grooming.

items.quote: But Siddhartha’s thoughts brought the Samana under their control

verdict.claim: The old Samana's blessing is given of his own free will.

items.explain: The blessing is forced, an irony about what Samana power is worth.

items.quote: After all, the world was sick

verdict.claim: The narrator calls the world sick as the Buddha rumour spreads.

items.explain: The narrator frames the rumour as medicine for a sick world.

items.quote: Yes, he thought, standing there with his head low, what would remain of all that which seemed to us to be holy?

verdict.claim: After Govinda's verse, Siddhartha's private thoughts restore his faith in all that is holy.

items.explain: Govinda's verse deepens Siddhartha's doubt instead of ending it.

items.quote: for hours and days he remained in the ____
items.explain: Hours in the 'non-self' always end in a return: the escape is real but temporary.

items.quote: had tasted the gloomy ____ of the cycle
items.explain: 'Intoxication' links meditation to the drinker's numbing in ¶13.

items.quote: he slipped out of his self into thousands of other ____
items.explain: 'Thousands of other forms' shows how far he flees the self, and still returns.

items.quote: There is indeed no such thing, so I believe, as what we refer to as ‘learning.’
items.explain: Siddhartha denies 'learning' itself, the paradox that will carry him past every teacher.

items.quote: comforting, mild, full of noble promises
items.explain: The narrator voices the rumour's sweetness while hinting it is only a 'seeming'.

items.quote: How should the Gotama’s teachings, even before we have heard them, have already revealed their best fruit to us?
items.explain: Govinda takes Siddhartha's riddle literally; the 'fruit' is leaving itself.

cards.text: Siddhartha says he is as far from wisdom as an unborn child
Govinda says the drinker has not become wiser
He likens it to the oxcart driver's rice wine
Govinda says a Samana is no drunkard
Siddhartha asks, 'What is meditation?'

items.explain: The argument's order shows Siddhartha winning the debate but not peace.

cards.text: The innermost being would awake
Once every desire is silent
His goal is to become empty
To be open to miracles
To be dead to himself

items.explain: The sentence climbs from emptiness to a hoped-for awakening.

cards.text: He asks not to be bothered with such talk
He asks about the sanctity of prayer
He asks what would become of all that is holy
Govinda stops and raises his hands
He says the words stir fear in his heart

items.explain: Govinda's protest moves from gesture to feeling to a defense of the sacred.

items.quote: loses himself in the meditation of **Atman**
items.explain: Atman is the true self within every being; Govinda's verse promises bliss in losing oneself in it.

items.quote: knew neither exercises nor **self-castigation**
items.explain: From Latin castigare, 'to chastise': enemies fault Gotama for skipping what the Samanas prize.

items.quote: Feverish dreams **flickered** from his enlarged eyes
items.explain: The unsteady light in his eyes shows the cost of his fasting.

items.quote: no one will find the path of paths?
items.link: Meditation, fasting and rice wine are named in ¶13 as brief escapes from the self; the path of paths is what 'we will not find' (¶20), as Govinda fearfully repeats (¶21).
items.explain: Three are escapes; the fourth is what they all fail to reach.

items.quote: I have asked the Brahmins, year after year
items.link: He 'asked' the Brahmins, the holy Vedas and the devoted Samanas (¶22); Atman is the one knowledge within everything, not a source he asked.
items.explain: He questioned teachers; the answer was within.

items.quote: where he could escape from the cycle, where the end of the causes
items.link: He waits for the place 'where he could escape from the cycle, where the end of the causes, where an eternity without suffering began' (¶6). A heron's death is part of the cycle.
items.explain: Three phrases name the release he hunts for; one is a trap of the cycle itself.

items.quote: It is hard, it is very hard to cast a spell on an old Samana.

verdict.claim: Govinda treats Siddhartha's spell as an easy trick any Samana could do.

items.explain: Govinda is awed by the feat; Siddhartha, in the next line, dismisses it.

items.quote: Unexpressable by words is his blissfulness of his heart.

verdict.claim: Govinda's verse says the bliss of Atman can be fully put into words.

items.explain: Govinda's own verse admits that the deepest bliss lies beyond words, which supports Siddhartha's doubt about teaching.

items.quote: a touch of sadness and a touch of mockery

verdict.claim: The narrator describes Siddhartha's laugh as purely joyful.

items.explain: The narrator's mixed laugh keeps Siddhartha both wise and wounded.
